lead.topic: Evolution of complex traits: firefly light-organ loss
lead.headline: Losing a firefly's glow rewires more than one gene
lead.deck: Genomes and gene knockdowns reveal how disappearing adult light organs coincide with lost gene families, changed regulation and altered cuticle development.
lead.authors: Fu X, Zhu X, Wu G
paragraphs: Some fireflies have given up flashing as adults, even though luminous relatives use light for courtship. To ask what disappears when a complex organ is lost, Xinhua Fu, Xinlei Zhu and Gang Wu compared the daytime, nonluminous firefly Pristolycus diversecostatus with the glowing Aquatica leii. They assembled a high-quality genome of the nonluminous species and combined gene-family comparisons with measurements of RNA expression and targeted gene knockdowns in its luminous relative. The comparison points to extensive gene-family contraction and changed expression across three metabolic modules associated with the missing adult light organ.

The team also focused on the organ's transparent outer covering, which lets the chemical light escape. In A. leii, reducing the activity of Laccase2, a gene linked to cuticle development, disrupted the adult light organ and its glow. Their analyses identified regulators of cuticle transparency and a network centered on homeobox transcription factors, proteins that coordinate development. The evidence connects genome change, gene regulation and physical organ structure, but comparing two species cannot establish the exact order of evolutionary losses. Gene interference in a living firefly demonstrates a requirement for normal development, not that changes to Laccase2 originally caused the disappearance of adult light.
lead.push: Does the loss of flashing begin with one regulatory switch, or accumulate through several gene losses? Sample additional independently nonluminous firefly lineages and compare light-organ gene expression across pupal stages. Restoring candidate regulators in nonluminous species, where technically possible, could distinguish irreversible structural losses from developmentally silent pathways retaining some capacity to produce light.

people.name: Xinhua Fu
people.bio: Xinhua Fu is a professor in the College of Plant Science and Technology at Huazhong Agricultural University in Wuhan. He holds a doctorate and studies firefly biodiversity, behavior, development and conservation. His research combines field surveys, taxonomy, firefly genome sequencing and investigations of the molecular mechanisms that control flashing.

people.name: Gang Wu
people.bio: Gang Wu is an associate professor of entomology at Huazhong Agricultural University, where he supervises master's students. He earned a doctorate at the Institute of Zoology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. His broader research addresses insect biodiversity monitoring, environmental change and invasive species, alongside collaborations on firefly developmental genomics.

slot2.headline: An AI-ready library catalogs a billion microbial peptides
slot2.cite: Yao et al., Nature Communications (13 Nov 2026). Research article.
slot2.body: Microbes manufacture an enormous variety of short proteins, many too small or unfamiliar for conventional annotation. Yao and colleagues assembled miProbe, a searchable collection of more than 1.08 billion nonredundant microbial peptides gathered from genomes and environmental sequencing data. They also provide over eight terabytes of precomputed embeddings, numerical representations generated by protein language models that let algorithms compare sequence patterns. The researchers report differences in peptide diversity among habitats and microbial groups and supply interfaces for downstream functional predictions. This resource could accelerate searches for antimicrobial compounds, but most cataloged peptides remain computational predictions, not experimentally verified molecules with established functions.

slot3.headline: X-rays create the defects that keep a crystal glowing
slot3.cite: Liu et al., Nature Communications (13 Nov 2026). Research article.
slot3.body: Many glowing materials keep emitting light after illumination ends because charge becomes trapped at defects in their crystals. Liu and colleagues discovered a different mechanism in bismuth-doped cesium zirconium chloride: X-rays make the material glow after exposure, whereas ultraviolet light does not. Their measurements indicate that X-rays create temporary missing chlorine atoms, known as vacancies, which trap charge and gradually heal. Adding tin changed how readily vacancies form and prolonged the afterglow to several hours. The researchers also embedded the crystals in a flexible film for X-ray imaging of curved objects. This is a laboratory materials demonstration, not a deployed medical scanner.

source_audit.title: Comparative genomics analysis of luminescent and non-luminescent fireflies reveals mechanisms underlying adult light organs development
source_audit.evidence: Verified publisher abstract, authors Fu, Zhu and Wu in that order, Nature Communications DOI and online date 13 Nov 2026. Abstract supports Pristolycus/Aquatica comparison, genome assembly, gene-family contraction, changed metabolic modules, RNA interference of Laccase2, cuticle transparency and homeobox regulators. Direct full-article HTML retrieval was unavailable, so no unstated effect sizes were inferred.

source_audit.title: Key homeobox transcription factors regulate the development of the firefly's adult light organ and bioluminescence
source_audit.evidence: Verified 2024 primary study of Aquatica leii homeobox regulators, organ development and luciferase; background, not the new study's results.

source_audit.title: miProbe: microbial peptide repository of biological embeddings
source_audit.evidence: Publisher abstract verifies 13 Nov 2026 publication, DOI, 1.08 billion microbial peptides, 8 TB of model embeddings, habitat diversity and API access. No laboratory verification of every peptide claimed.

source_audit.title: Dynamic chlorine vacancies enable X-ray-specific afterglow
source_audit.evidence: Publisher abstract verifies 13 Nov 2026, DOI, bismuth-doped cesium zirconium chloride, X-ray-specific temporary chlorine vacancies, tin-modulated multiple-hour afterglow and flexible imaging film. Laboratory demonstration distinguished from clinical deployment.
